text: CSDM doesn't store everything in one flat pile. It groups CMDB data into a small number of layers, each with its own job. In this lesson we'll walk through those layers conceptually — what belongs in each one, and why keeping them separate actually matters.

At the base sits foundational, shared data — locations, companies, business units, and the core infrastructure CIs from Chapters 1 and 2: servers, databases, network devices. A second layer holds design-time planning data — services and applications being proposed or built but not yet live. On top sits the live, operational layer: the services and CIs actually running in production right now, the ones Incident and Problem management care about.

Foundational data is the base everything else depends on — you can't model a service meaningfully until the locations and infrastructure it runs on already exist as clean records. Planning-layer data is real and worth tracking, but it describes intent and future state, not what's live today. Operational data is what's actually running — outages here affect real users right now.

Over time, a given piece of planning data is expected to move toward production: a proposed service gets approved, gets built, and eventually gets deployed and promoted into the live, operational layer. The planning layer and the operational layer describe stages in that same lifecycle, not two unrelated buckets.

Without this separation, a CMDB easily ends up conflating what's being planned with what's actually running — confusing impact analysis, which should only trace through what's genuinely live, and confusing portfolio planning, which needs visibility into what's still in the pipeline without production noise mixed in. Keeping these layers distinct, built on the same foundational data, is what lets planners, support engineers, and executives each trust that what they're looking at is scoped correctly.

Next, we'll zoom into one specific, important distinction inside this model: the difference between a Business Service and a Technical Service, and why that distinction is what lets you answer "what breaks" in terms the business actually understands.
